source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: The opening links received eyewitness testimony, the writer's careful inquiry, an orderly account, and reliable instruction. ‘Orderly’ does not by itself specify a strictly chronological arrangement.
‘Fathers' hearts’ retains the family language of the Greek. The saying links turning within families with the disobedient turning toward righteous wisdom.
Elizabeth speaks of disgrace ‘among people.’ The narrator has already called both her and Zechariah righteous in verse 6.
‘Favored one’ describes someone who has received favor or grace. The text followed here does not add ‘blessed are you among women’ to this greeting; that blessing occurs in verse 42.
The Greek can also be construed ‘the holy child to be born will be called Son of God.’ ‘Overshadow’ retains the source's image without explaining a mechanism.
‘No word from God will fail’ can also be rendered more broadly, ‘Nothing will be impossible with God.’ The word translated ‘word’ can also refer to a matter or event.
The Greek term is the feminine form of ‘slave.’ Mary uses it of herself; her spoken assent in verse 38 is also retained.
The clause can be read as the content of belief, as here, or as its ground: ‘blessed is she who believed, because there will be a fulfillment.’
A horn is an image of strength; ‘horn of salvation’ preserves the song's ancient image of saving power.
The Greek word can mean rising or dawn. The following light imagery supports ‘dawn’ here; the verb in the text followed is future, ‘will visit.’
vocabulary: Lowly condition or humiliation; a person's circumstances, not necessarily a claim to humility as a virtue.
Release or forgiveness; here release from sins.

notes: The text is rendered ‘first registration’ and ‘when Quirinius was governing Syria.’ The wording is not changed to ‘before Quirinius’ to resolve a chronological question.
‘Guest room’ can also mean ‘lodging place.’ The verse does not describe the building's layout or mention an innkeeper.
The Greek reading followed here means people of favor or goodwill, understood as recipients of God's favor. Another reading underlies the familiar ‘goodwill toward people.’
The Greek has the plural ‘their purification.’ The translation does not change this to ‘her purification.’
The text followed here says ‘his father and mother.’ The word ‘father’ is retained alongside the preceding birth account.
The sword saying interrupts the prophecy about opposition and the disclosure of hearts. ‘Fall and rising’ does not specify whether the same people experience both.
Eighty-four is taken here as Anna's age. The construction can also be understood as eighty-four years of widowhood.
The Greek can mean ‘in my Father's house’ or, more broadly, ‘engaged in my Father's affairs.’ The temple setting supports ‘house’ here.
The term rendered ‘stature’ can also refer to age or maturity.
vocabulary: Inhabited world; here used within an imperial decree.
Master / slave; the paired terms in Simeon's address.
Must or it is necessary; repeated in Jesus' account of his mission in 4:43.

notes: The dating frame names imperial, regional, and priestly authorities before locating the word of God with John in the wilderness.
John addresses the crowds in Luke's account. The translation does not replace them with a narrower group from another Gospel.
The soldiers are not assigned a national identity in this verse. Both coercion and false accusation are prohibited.
Spirit and fire remain together in the baptism saying; the following threshing image includes both gathering and burning.
‘When he began’ is elliptical; the beginning of Jesus' public work is understood. ‘As people supposed’ qualifies his being Joseph's son.
The repeated ‘son of’ makes the backward chain of descent clear. The genealogy is not altered to match another biblical list.
‘Joshua’ renders the Greek name Iēsous, the same Greek form used for ‘Jesus.’
The pinned Greek text has the name forms Jobel and Sala and includes both Admin and Arni. These are preserved rather than silently replaced from a parallel genealogy.
Cainan, written Kainam in this Greek text, appears in two different positions in the genealogy. Both occurrences are retained.
vocabulary: Tetrarch, a title for a regional ruler.
Repentance, a turning or change of mind and direction.
Winnowing fork, a tool for tossing threshed grain to separate it from chaff.
In bodily form; Luke's wording for the Spirit's visible descent.

notes: The shorter bread quotation and Luke's sequence of tests are retained. The Greek text here does not name a mountain in verse 5 or add a dismissal of Satan in verse 8.
The claim about receiving and distributing authority is the devil's speech, not a separate assertion by the narrator.
The temple's ‘highest point’ renders a term literally related to a wing or projecting edge. The verse does not identify its precise location.
The quotation includes good news, release, sight, freedom for the oppressed, and favor. The text followed here does not add ‘to heal the brokenhearted.’
‘Gracious words’ can also be understood as ‘words of grace,’ emphasizing their content as well as their manner.
‘Leprosy’ represents an ancient disease term; it does not establish a modern medical diagnosis.
Jesus rebukes the fever. The narrator does not call the fever a demon.
The Greek text followed here reads ‘Judea.’ Another reading has ‘Galilee.’ The geographical wording is not harmonized to the preceding scenes.
vocabulary: Release or forgiveness; the same word rendered ‘forgiveness’ in 1:77 and 3:3.
Acceptable, favorable, or welcome; used of the Lord's year and a prophet's reception.
Authority; repeated in the response to the unclean spirit's departure.
